question: Why do the dust storms that wrap all of Mars start in the southern hemisphere's spring or summer?
answer: Because Mars is then closest to the Sun. Its orbit is stretched enough that sunlight at the nearest point is about 45% stronger than at the farthest, and the nearest point falls in late southern spring. Extra heat drives stronger winds, which lift dust, which soaks up more sunlight: a storm that feeds itself.
move: An uneven input can make one season far wilder than its mirror.
ask: Do I expect two sides of my life to behave the same when one gets more input?
source: Zurek and Martin, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1993
reference: Zurek and Martin, Interannual variability of planet-encircling dust storms on Mars, Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets 98(E2), 1993
